extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers of Kant and metaphysics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual distinctions for assessing teleological and moral proofs concerning God, freedom, and immortality — distinguishing theoretical versus practical (moral) grounds of conviction and the limits of analogy, probability, hypothesis, and syllogistic proof for supersensible objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof should not persuade but convince
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requisite for every proof ... It should not persuade, but convince, or at least should tend to conviction. I.e. the ground of proof or the conclusion should not be merely a subjective (aesthetical) determining ground of assent (mere illusion), but objectively valid and a logical ground of cognition; for otherwise the Understanding is ensnared, but not convinced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid merely stirring feelings or rhetorical persuasion (subjective/aesthetical grounds). A valid proof must contain objective logical grounds that can bear strict examination rather than produce mere persuasion or wholesome illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish persuasion from conviction (and kinds of conviction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish what merely belongs to persuasion from that which leads to conviction (for these are determinations of assent which differ not merely in degree but in kind). A proof which is intended to convince can again be of two kinds; either deciding what the object is in itself, or what it is for us ... (κατ’ ἀλήθειαν or κατ’ ἄνθρωπον).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proof, state whether it aims at theoretical (object-in-itself) conviction or practical/reflective (what it is for us) conviction; do not conflate these aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not blend physical and moral teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: The division of the proof into the two dissimilar parts involved in the argument—belonging to physical and moral Teleology respectively—cannot and must not be prevented. For the blending of these makes it impossible to discern where the proper force of the proof lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep arguments from physical purposiveness (natural teleology) and moral purposiveness (practical teleology) separate so that weaknesses/strengths of each can be clearly assessed and elaborated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of theoretical grounds of proof (and their hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: All theoretical grounds of proof resolve themselves either into: (1) Proofs by logically strict Syllogisms of Reason; or where this is not the case, (2) Conclusions according to analogy; or where this also has no place, (3) Probable opinion; or finally, (4) Assumption of a merely possible ground of explanation, i.e. Hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or evaluating proofs, identify which type of ground is being used and subject it to the appropriate standards — syllogism requires strict logic, analogy is limited, opinion lacks a priori place, hypothesis requires secure possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic/theoretical proof cannot establish supersensible existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Since no intuition possible for us corresponds to the concept of a Being that is to be sought beyond nature ... there is absolutely no cognition of it to be had (by which the extent of our theoretical knowledge is in the least enlarged). The particular concept of a supersensible Being cannot be subsumed under the universal principles of the nature of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect deductive/theoretical syllogisms based on empirical or natural principles to yield cognitive proof of God or the immortal soul; the necessary intuitions and predicates are lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of analogical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: We can indeed think one of two dissimilar things ... in accordance with the analogy of the other; but we cannot, from that wherein they are dissimilar, conclude from the one to the other by analogy, i.e. transfer from the one to the other this sign of specific distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy can help conceive a supersensible cause analogously to human understanding (e.g., works of art), but cannot justify transferring specific material or distinctive properties from familiar cases to a transcendent Being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability has no place for judgements about the supersensible grounded in experience
rubrics_metrics.description: If the given grounds of proof from which we start (as here from the purposes in the world) are empirical, then we cannot even with their aid form any opinion as to anything beyond the world of sense, nor can we concede to such venturesome judgements the smallest claim to probability. For probability is part of a certainty possible in a certain series of grounds ... one part cannot lie within experience and another outside all possible experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat empirical evidence about nature as conferring probabilistic support for claims about supersensible realities; mixing experiential and transcendent grounds makes probability incoherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis requires the possibility of its basis to be certain
rubrics_metrics.description: If an hypothesis is to serve for the explanation of the possibility of a given phenomenon, at least its possibility must be completely certain. The possibility of that which I place at the basis of my explanation, must at least be exposed to no doubt; otherwise there would be no end of empty chimeras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking hypotheses to explain phenomena, ensure that the hypothesis's possibility is indisputable; speculative assumptions about supersensible beings fail this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: No theoretical proof can produce belief in God's existence or soul's immortality
rubrics_metrics.description: For the existence [Dasein] of the original Being, as a Godhead, or of the soul as an immortal spirit, absolutely no proof in a theoretical point of view is possible for the human Reason, which can bring about even the least degree of belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the theoretical limits: absence of adequate material/intuitions means theoretical reason cannot establish belief in supersensible objects; other modes (practical) are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of cognisable things: opinion, fact, faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognisable things are of three kinds: things of opinion (opinabile); things of fact (scibile); and things of faith (mere credibile). Objects of mere rational Ideas ... are not cognisable things; objects whose objective reality can be proved are things of fact; objects required by pure practical Reason and transcendent for theory are things of faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, place them into one of these categories: opinable (empirically inaccessible but conceivable), scibile (empirically or rationally demonstrable), or res fidei (practically postulated — e.g., God, immortality, highest good). This determines what kind of justification is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom and highest good as things of fact/faith depending on role
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one rational Idea ... which also comes under things of fact. This is the Idea of freedom, whose reality ... may be exhibited by means of practical laws of pure Reason, and conformably to this, in actual actions, and, consequently, in experience. ... The highest final purpose to be worked out by us ... is an Idea which has in a practical reference objective reality for us ... it is a mere thing of faith of the pure Reason, along with God and Immortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat freedom differently — its practical effects can be exhibited and count as a scibile in experience — whereas the highest good, God, and immortality are postulated as res fidei for moral practical purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral faith as a practical postulate (habitus) justified by duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith (as habitus, not as act) is the moral attitude of Reason as to belief in that which is unattainable by theoretical cognition. It is therefore the constant principle of the mind, to assume as true, on account of the obligation in reference to it, that which it is necessary to presuppose as condition of the possibility of the highest moral final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral faith is justified as a necessary practical presupposition for pursuing the highest moral ends; it is a settled orientation (habitus) rather than a theoretical proof-based assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reality of ideas despite theoretical indeterminacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus this Idea gains practical reality, although all means of creating such for it in a theoretical point of view, for the explanation of nature and determination of the supreme Cause, are entirely wanting for speculative cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some ideas (e.g., God as moral Author) can be practically real and necessary for moral life even if they lack theoretical justification; use them regulatively to govern conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral argument's corrective uses for theology and religion
rubrics_metrics.description: The limitation of Reason ... has, as far as the Idea of God is concerned, undeniable uses. For it prevents Theology from rising into Theosophy ... or from sinking into Demonology ... It also prevents Religion from turning into Theurgy ... or into Idolatry ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the moral framing of ideas to avoid speculative excesses and fanatical or superstitious distortions — moral postulates regulate theology's practical function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulative vs constitutive principles for reflective vs determinant judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: We can only assume this distinction as subjectively necessary by the constitution of our cognitive faculties, and as valid for the reflective, not for the objectively determinant Judgement. ... but as a principle for judging of the objective possibility of things, it is no way theoretically determinant ... but is a mere regulative principle for the reflective Judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking ideas or principles, specify whether they function as regulative (guiding inquiry/reflection) or constitutive (asserting objective determination); do not treat regulative principles as if they constituted objective knowledge.
